## Candidate 01 — Posterior Updating as Beta Curves Transform Through a Fixed Data Sequence

- Source: `math-bayesian-probability/chapters/08-when-data-is-sparse.md`
- Topic: Bayesian updating · Beta-Binomial conjugacy
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: A flat "I know nothing" prior — Beta(1,1) — visibly swallows data event by event and sharpens into a tight posterior you never would have guessed from the starting shape.
- The rule: Conjugate Beta-Binomial update — Beta(α, β) + k successes in n trials → Beta(α+k, β+n−k). Posterior mean = (α+k)/(α+β+n).
- Concrete numbers: Start at Beta(1,1) flat prior. Scripted sequence: observe 3 complications in 200 trials (medical QA scenario). Intermediate checkpoints at k=0 (prior), k=1/n=67, k=2/n=133, k=3/n=200. Also animate the informative-prior version: Beta(3,200) → Beta(6,397), showing how a tighter prior resists the data less dramatically.
- The artifact / what moves: The Beta(α,β) probability density curve morphs continuously from a flat rectangle (Beta(1,1)), bulging and sharpening event by event toward a tall, narrow peak near p=0.015 as each trial's data lands. A running text ticker shows current α, β, and posterior mean. A second curve (the informative prior) tracks in a contrasting color, showing its smaller shift — the shrinkage differential drawn live.
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: After 3 successes in 200 trials from a flat prior, posterior mean = 4/203 ≈ 0.0197 and 95% CrI upper bound ≈ 0.044 — verifiable from the Beta(4,198) CDF. P2: With the informative prior Beta(3,200), posterior mean = 6/403 ≈ 0.0149 — shrinkage toward 1.47% rather than the MLE 1.5%; posterior is visibly narrower than flat-prior case.
- The change: Swap the data sequence to 8 complications in 200 trials — watch the flat-prior posterior jump to mean ≈ 4% while the informative Beta(3,200) prior pulls it back to ≈ 2.2%, making the shrinkage gap dramatic and visible.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: Shrinkage is not smoothing or censorship — it is the prior's evidence voting against extreme observations. The animation shows exactly how much voting power the prior has relative to data count.
- Exclusions: Do not animate MCMC sampling or trace plots; do not show credible intervals as error bars — draw the full curve.
- Sim slug: bayesian-beta-binomial-update
- Score: 10/10

## Candidate 02 — Bayes' Theorem Base-Rate Inversion: Prior Sweeping from Rare to Common

- Source: `math-bayesian-probability/chapters/01-the-same-question-two-answers.md`
- Topic: Bayes' theorem · base-rate neglect
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: A 99%-accurate test still delivers a posterior of only 9% when the disease is rare — and watching the posterior rise as prevalence sweeps from 0.1% to 10% makes this feel inevitable rather than paradoxical.
- The rule: P(disease | positive) = P(positive|disease)·P(disease) / [P(positive|disease)·P(disease) + P(positive|no disease)·P(no disease)]. With sensitivity=0.99 and FPR=0.01.
- Concrete numbers: Sensitivity=0.99, FPR=0.01. Scripted prevalence sweep: 0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.50. Posterior at each: ≈9%, 33%, 50%, 84%, 91%, 99%. Fixed reference: prevalence=0.001 → posterior≈0.0902.
- The artifact / what moves: A vertical bar chart divides the population of 10,000 into true-positive, false-positive, true-negative, false-negative rectangles. As prevalence sweeps upward, the TP rectangle grows while the FP rectangle shrinks, and a live label shows the current posterior. A second panel draws a P(disease|positive) vs prevalence curve, with the current value highlighted as a dot tracing the curve from left to right.
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: At prevalence=0.001 with sensitivity=0.99 and FPR=0.01, posterior=(0.001×0.99)/((0.001×0.99)+(0.999×0.01))=0.00099/0.01098≈0.0902. P2: The posterior reaches 0.50 at prevalence≈0.01 (1%) — the crossover point where true-positives equal false-positives — verifiable analytically by setting numerator=denominator in Bayes' formula.
- The change: Vary FPR from 0.01 to 0.001 while holding prevalence=0.001 — posterior jumps from 9% to ≈50%, showing that halving the false positive rate has far more impact at low prevalence than halving disease rarity.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: Accuracy is not a single number — it is a pair of conditional probabilities that interact with base rates. The animation forces the viewer to watch the interaction happening in real time.
- Exclusions: Do not animate ROC curves or AUC; do not add sliders (D3 territory); scripted prevalence sequence only.
- Sim slug: bayesian-base-rate-inversion
- Score: 10/10

## Candidate 03 — Beta Distribution Shape Morphing: α and β Sweeping Through Behavioral Regimes

- Source: `math-bayesian-probability/chapters/08-when-data-is-sparse.md`
- Topic: Beta distribution · parameter geometry
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: The same distribution family produces a bathtub, a uniform, a hill, and a spike at a corner — and watching α and β navigate this shape space makes conjugate priors feel like a controllable instrument rather than a formula.
- The rule: Beta(α,β) PDF: f(p) = p^(α−1)·(1−p)^(β−1)/B(α,β) where B(α,β)=Γ(α)Γ(β)/Γ(α+β). Mean=α/(α+β).
- Concrete numbers: Scripted tour of parameter space — (1,1): flat; (0.5,0.5): U-shaped bathtub; (2,2): symmetric hill; (2,8): skewed left; (8,2): skewed right; (50,50): tight peak at 0.5; (3,200): sharp spike near zero (the medical-QA prior from Ch.8). All eight shown as a guided sequence with named labels.
- The artifact / what moves: A single PDF curve morphs continuously through all eight parameter configurations in order, with the current α and β values displayed as animated digits, and the mean location marked by a vertical tick that moves along the x-axis as mean=α/(α+β) changes. The curve's peak height visually rises and falls as the distribution concentrates.
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: At α=β=1, the distribution is exactly flat (uniform PDF=1 everywhere on [0,1]) — the curve should be a horizontal line at height 1. P2: At α=50, β=50, mean=0.5 and the 95% highest-density interval is approximately [0.43, 0.57] — the curve should be so tall and narrow that the x-axis extends visibly beyond it on both sides.
- The change: Animate α increasing from 1 to 50 while β is held fixed at 2 — the mode traces from 0 to near 1, showing how the "successes" parameter alone steers the distribution's peak location.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: Choosing a prior is choosing where in this shape space to start — the animation makes visible how much you commit to when you write Beta(3,200) vs Beta(1,1).
- Exclusions: Do not explain the gamma function derivation; do not animate sampling from the distribution (D3 territory).
- Sim slug: beta-distribution-shape-tour
- Score: 9/10

## Candidate 04 — Normal Posterior Shrinkage: Three Priors Compressing Toward the Same Limit

- Source: `math-bayesian-probability/chapters/07-priors.md`
- Topic: Conjugate Normal update · prior sensitivity
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: Three analysts, same data, three conclusions — and doubling the sample size makes all three converge to the same answer. Watching that convergence removes the "Bayesian is subjective" objection in ten seconds.
- The rule: Normal-Normal conjugate update. Posterior mean = (μ_prior/σ²_prior + x̄/σ²_data) / (1/σ²_prior + 1/σ²_data). Posterior precision = 1/σ²_prior + n/σ².
- Concrete numbers: Three priors on treatment effect δ: (1) flat/improper → posterior = data; (2) Normal(0,10²) weakly informative; (3) Normal(0,2²) informative. Data: n=40, δ̄=4.9 mmHg, SE=2.3. Posterior means: 4.9, 4.75, 2.11. Scripted n sequence: n=10, 40, 200, 400 — show all three posteriors converging.
- The artifact / what moves: Three Gaussian curves (one per prior) drawn side by side on the same axis, each centered at its posterior mean. As the scripted n increases through the four values, all three curves narrow and migrate toward each other — at n=400, they are nearly indistinguishable. The spread between their centers shrinks visibly with each step, and a live label shows the current sample size.
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: With informative prior Normal(0,4) and data SE=2.3 at n=40, posterior mean = (4.9×0.189)/(0.189+0.25) ≈ 2.11 mmHg — verifiable by the conjugate formula. P2: At n=400 (SE≈0.73 mmHg), all three posterior means differ by less than 0.1 mmHg — the prior is washed out, verifiable analytically since the data precision 1/0.73²≈1.88 swamps even the tight prior precision 0.25.
- The change: Hold n=40 fixed but make the informative prior even tighter — Normal(0,1²) instead of Normal(0,2²) — showing the posterior mean pulled further to 1.0 mmHg and P(δ>3) falling below 0.10.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: Prior sensitivity is finite — it disappears with enough data. The animation reveals the exact n at which the debate about priors becomes empirically irrelevant.
- Exclusions: Do not animate MCMC chains; do not draw credible intervals as whiskers — use full posterior curves throughout.
- Sim slug: normal-posterior-prior-shrinkage
- Score: 9/10

## Candidate 05 — Sequential Bayesian Updating: "Today's Posterior Is Tomorrow's Prior" Drawn Live

- Source: `math-bayesian-probability/chapters/10-time-and-sequence.md`
- Topic: Sequential Bayesian updating · structural time series
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: Each new week's demand reading visibly reshapes a probability curve — and you can watch the posterior tighten and migrate over 12 weeks, making the abstract "posterior becomes prior" principle into something you can see happen.
- The rule: Normal-Normal sequential update. At each step: posterior_t+1 mean = (μ_t/σ²_t + y_t+1/σ²_obs) / (1/σ²_t + 1/σ²_obs); posterior variance updates as 1/(1/σ²_t + 1/σ²_obs).
- Concrete numbers: σ²_obs = 1,633² (from ARIMA prediction interval in chapter). Week 1 prior: Normal(8,000, 800²). Scripted sequence: 12 weekly observations from 8,000→11,000 trend. After 12 updates: posterior ≈ Normal(10,840, ~500²). Threshold line at 10,000 units with live P(demand>10,000) annotation.
- The artifact / what moves: A Normal probability density curve plotted on a demand axis (x-axis: 5,000–16,000 units). At each weekly step, the curve visibly shifts right (mean rising) and narrows (uncertainty shrinking). The 10,000-unit threshold is a fixed vertical line, and the shaded area to its right shrinks then expands as data arrives, with a live percentage label showing P(demand>10,000) at each step.
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: After 6 updates with consistent upward trend, P(demand>10,000) should cross 0.50 — verifiable by computing the midpoint of the demand trajectory. P2: After 12 updates, posterior SD should be less than σ_obs/√12 ≈ 471 — the standard error of a running mean, verifiable from the conjugate formula.
- The change: Introduce one anomalous outlier week (demand=7,000 in week 8) — the posterior mean jumps left, P(demand>10,000) temporarily drops, then recovers as subsequent normal-trend weeks pull it back. Shows Bayesian updating is not immune to outliers.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: The week-by-week update makes "sequential Bayesian inference" lose its abstraction — the update is just arithmetic applied to a curve, and you watch it do its job.
- Exclusions: Do not animate the ARIMA model or its ACF/PACF; do not show trace plots; keep to the Normal-Normal closed-form animation.
- Sim slug: bayesian-sequential-updating
- Score: 8/10

## Candidate 06 — Gaussian Posterior Narrowing: Credible Interval Contracting as n Increases

- Source: `math-bayesian-probability/chapters/04-comparing-two-groups.md`
- Topic: Posterior precision · credible interval convergence
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: The 95% credible interval for a treatment effect starts wide enough to be useless, but shrinks to a useful width at a specific n — and you can watch the threshold where evidence becomes actionable appear.
- The rule: Posterior for Normal likelihood: SD_posterior = 1/√(1/σ²_prior + n/σ²). 95% CrI = posterior_mean ± 1.96×SD_posterior.
- Concrete numbers: Tutorial comparison scenario. Prior: Normal(0,15²) on δ=μ_B−μ_A. Within-group SD σ=8. Scripted n sequence per group: 5, 10, 20, 38, 80, 200, 500. At n=38: 95% CrI ≈ [0.2, 7.6] (width 7.4 pts). At n=200: width ≈ 3.2 pts. At n=500: width ≈ 2.0 pts. Decision threshold: CrI width < 3 points = "actionable."
- The artifact / what moves: A Normal posterior curve drawn around the observed effect (δ̄=4 points), with the 95% region shaded. As n steps through the sequence, the shaded region visibly contracts symmetrically — a live label shows "n per group = X" and "CrI width = Y pts." A horizontal dashed line at width=3 marks the "actionable" threshold; the shaded region shrinks through it at n≈200.
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: At n=38 per group with σ=8 and weakly informative prior, SD_posterior ≈ 8/√38 ≈ 1.3, giving CrI width ≈ 5.1 points (match chapter's [0.2, 7.6] range). P2: At n=200 per group, SD_posterior ≈ 8/√200 ≈ 0.566, CrI width ≈ 2.2 points — verifiable from the formula.
- The change: Add a competing informative prior Normal(0,2²) showing that with a tight prior, the CrI at n=38 is already narrower — making the "how much does prior choice matter at each n?" question visually answerable.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: Sample-size calculations in frequentist power analysis become posterior-width calculations in Bayesian planning — the animation shows these are the same question asked differently.
- Exclusions: Do not animate the data themselves as dot plots; do not show p-value annotations.
- Sim slug: bayesian-credible-interval-narrowing
- Score: 8/10

## Candidate 07 — Hierarchical Shrinkage: School Estimates Pulled Toward the Grand Mean

- Source: `math-bayesian-probability/chapters/09-hierarchical-problems.md`
- Topic: Bayesian hierarchical models · partial pooling
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: A school with 8 students scores 92% — but the hierarchical model disagrees, pulling the estimate down to 83%. Watching the pull happen across 30 schools simultaneously reveals why partial pooling is not a bug.
- The rule: Partial-pooling shrinkage: BLUP/posterior mean for school j = λ_j × x̄_j + (1−λ_j) × μ_district, where λ_j = σ²_district/(σ²_district + σ²_within/n_j) is the "reliability" of school j's estimate.
- Concrete numbers: District parameters: μ_district=72%, σ_between=6.5%, σ_within=8.2%. Scripted schools: A(n=200, raw=74.2%, posterior=74.0%), B(n=12, raw=81.5%, posterior=79.2%), C(n=8, raw=92%, posterior=83.1%), D(n=6, raw=61%, posterior=67.4%). Shrinkage factor λ_C = 6.5²/(6.5²+8.2²/8) = 42.25/50.65 ≈ 0.83 → pulled 17% toward mean.
- The artifact / what moves: A horizontal dot plot of all 30 schools' raw means (open circles) and posterior estimates (filled circles), connected by arrows. Schools with large n have short arrows (little pull); schools with small n have long arrows pointing toward the district mean (dashed vertical line at 72%). The animation draws each school's arrow in sequence, sorted by n descending — large schools first (barely moved), small schools last (dramatically pulled).
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: School C (n=8, raw=92%) pulls to posterior≈83.1% — the shrinkage formula gives λ_C≈0.83, so estimate = 0.83×92 + 0.17×72 = 76.36+12.24 = 88.6% (note: exact calculation requires the Gelman hierarchical example parameters; verify against the chapter's reported 83.1%). P2: School A (n=200, raw=74.2%) pulls to posterior≈74.0% — less than 0.3% shrinkage — because with 200 observations the school-level data dominates the grand mean.
- The change: Double σ_between from 6.5% to 13% — schools become more spread out, shrinkage decreases (each school's raw mean is trusted more), and the arrows shorten across the board.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: Pooling is a bet on similarity across groups. The animation makes the bet visible: small-n schools are pulled hard because they must borrow from neighbors; large-n schools refuse the pull.
- Exclusions: Do not animate MCMC sampling; do not show trace plots or credible interval overlaps — the dot plot with arrows is the animation.
- Sim slug: hierarchical-shrinkage-schools
- Score: 7/10

## Candidate 08 — Logistic Curve Drawing: Log-Odds Sweeping to an S-Curve

- Source: `math-bayesian-probability/chapters/11-classification-and-decision.md`
- Topic: Logistic regression · decision threshold geometry
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: The threshold at 0.5 is almost never the right threshold — and the decision boundary sliding along the logistic curve shows exactly what cost ratio it implies.
- The rule: P(Y=1|x) = 1/(1+e^(−(β₀+β₁x))). Optimal threshold under asymmetric costs: c* = C_FN/(C_FN+C_FP) where C_FN is cost of false negative and C_FP is cost of false positive.
- Concrete numbers: From chapter: intercept β₀=−2.84, single feature (debt-to-income) β₁=1.73. Cost ratio 5:1 (false negative 5× more costly than false positive). Optimal threshold c* = 5/(5+1) ≈ 0.833 → NOT 0.5. Scripted cost ratio sequence: 1:1 (c*=0.5), 2:1 (c*=0.67), 5:1 (c*=0.83), 10:1 (c*=0.91).
- The artifact / what moves: The logistic S-curve draws from left to right as debt-to-income increases. A horizontal threshold line starts at 0.5, then rises through the four cost-ratio configurations in sequence. As the threshold rises, the "approve" region on the x-axis shrinks and a live label shows the current cost ratio and resulting threshold value. A shaded region below the curve shows the approve/decline split shifting in real time.
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: At cost ratio 5:1, optimal threshold c*=5/6≈0.833 — derivable from the Bayesian decision theory formula: decline when P(default|x) > C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN). P2: At the default threshold 0.5, a borrower with debt-to-income=0 has estimated default probability = 1/(1+e^2.84)≈0.055 — well below the threshold, correctly approved — verifiable from the logistic formula.
- The change: Flip the cost ratio to 1:5 (false positive 5× more costly than false negative — regulatory penalty regime) — threshold drops below 0.2, nearly all applicants approved, showing the threshold's regulatory interpretation made explicit.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: The default 0.5 threshold encodes an invisible assumption that loan loss and missed-revenue cost the same — the animation makes that assumption visible by showing what cost ratio would justify any threshold.
- Exclusions: Do not animate full coefficient distributions or posterior MCMC; do not show ROC curve.
- Sim slug: logistic-decision-threshold-geometry
- Score: 7/10

## Candidate 09 — Posterior Predictive Distribution Tracing: Regression Confidence vs. Prediction Band

- Source: `math-bayesian-probability/chapters/05-regression-both-ways.md`
- Topic: Bayesian regression · posterior predictive distribution
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: The confidence band tells you where the regression line is; the prediction band tells you where a new observation will fall — and watching both grow as advertising spend extrapolates beyond the data makes the difference viscerally clear.
- The rule: Posterior predictive for new x*: ỹ* ~ Normal(α+β·x*, σ²+Var(α+β·x*)). The prediction band is always wider than the confidence band by σ (residual SD). Bayesian version includes parameter uncertainty in both.
- Concrete numbers: Slope β̂=2.3 (SE=0.4), intercept α̂=124.7 (SE=8.2), σ≈18. At x*=current spend (x̄=40): 95% CI for mean ≈ [±1.96×SE_mean] ≈ ±6; 95% prediction interval ≈ [±1.96×√(σ²+SE²)] ≈ ±36. The two bands differ by a factor of 6.
- The artifact / what moves: A scatter plot of 60 data points with the fitted regression line drawn first. Then two shaded bands grow outward from the line — the narrow confidence band (uncertainty about the line position) and the wide prediction band (uncertainty about where a new point will land). As a probe point moves rightward beyond the data range to x=extrapolation territory, both bands widen but the prediction band always exceeds the CI by σ — shown as an animated gap labeled "residual uncertainty."
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: At the mean of x (x=40), SE of the fitted mean is minimized — the confidence band is narrowest there; both bands widen symmetrically as x moves away from x̄, verifiable from the OLS prediction variance formula. P2: The prediction interval width always exceeds the confidence interval width by at least 2×1.96×σ (where σ≈18 here) — the gap is ≈71 units regardless of x position.
- The change: Animate the effect of doubling n from 60 to 120 weeks — the confidence band shrinks by 1/√2 but the prediction band barely changes (residual σ dominates for individual predictions), showing why more data helps the mean estimate but cannot tame observation noise.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: The prediction band is the honest deliverable for a one-quarter forecast decision; the confidence band is the honest deliverable for a policy question about the slope — confusing them is the source of most forecast overconfidence.
- Exclusions: Do not animate posterior sampling chains; do not show frequentist vs Bayesian bands as separate animation — focus on the CI vs PI gap.
- Sim slug: bayesian-regression-predictive-bands
- Score: 6/10
